choices.text: In the extracellular space around the cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: In the periplasmic space of the organism

choices.label: D
choices.text: On the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane

choices.label: E
choices.text: Within the mature peptidoglycan layer itself

explanation.summary: NAG and NAM are synthesized in the cytoplasm and then transported out to the cell wall.
explanation.whyCorrect: The glycans NAG and NAM are made in the cytoplasm of the cell and then eventually transported to the cell wall in three steps using the lipid carrier bactoprenol. This is why a lipid carrier is required at all: the sugars must cross a membrane.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Synthesis occurs inside the cell, not in the extracellular space.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The periplasm lies outside the plasma membrane; the sugars are made before they reach it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The membrane surface is where NAM is loaded onto bactoprenol, not where the glycans are synthesized.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The peptidoglycan layer is the destination of the glycans, not their site of synthesis.

questions.stem: Once chains of peptidoglycan have been constructed, they are joined to one another through their peptide chains so that multiple layers form a rigid network. Which enzymes carry out this cross-linking?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autolysins

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bactoprenol synthases

choices.label: C
choices.text: Beta-lactamases

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transglycosylases

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transpeptidases

explanation.summary: Transpeptidases cross-link peptidoglycan chains through their peptide bridges, creating the rigid multilayer wall.
explanation.whyCorrect: After the glycan chains are built, transpeptidases cross-link them to each other through peptide chains. This cross-linking allows multiple layers to develop in the cell wall, forming the rigid network that gives the bacterium its structural integrity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autolysin activity cleaves wall material at the growing point rather than forming peptide cross-links.
whyWrongByChoice.B: No such enzyme is described as performing peptide cross-linking in the cell wall.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Beta-lactamases are bacterial resistance enzymes that destroy antibiotics; they do not build the wall.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Transglycosylase activity forms the new glycoside bonds of the sugar backbone, not the peptide cross-links.

questions.stem: A staphylococcal isolate is exposed to vancomycin in vitro. Elongation of its peptidoglycan and cross-linking of the chains are both inhibited. Which of the following best describes the outcome for the organism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cell lysis, so that the drug is bactericidal

choices.label: B
choices.text: Conversion of the organism to a dormant spore-forming state

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased drug efflux with no change in wall architecture

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reversible growth arrest that resolves when drug is removed

choices.label: E
choices.text: Selective loss of ribosomal protein synthesis without lysis

explanation.summary: Blocking peptidoglycan elongation and cross-linking leads to cell lysis, making vancomycin bactericidal.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because the newly formed NAM-NAG unit cannot be added to the chain, the peptidoglycan cannot grow and the chains cannot be cross-linked. The resulting failure of wall integrity leads to cell lysis, which is why vancomycin is a bactericidal agent.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Sporulation is not the described response to peptidoglycan inhibition.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Efflux without structural change would mean the drug had no effect, which contradicts the lysis described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reversible growth arrest describes a bacteriostatic drug; vancomycin kills the organism outright.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vancomycin does not act on the ribosome or protein synthesis.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man asks a pharmacist about bacitracin. Which of the following describes the typical clinical use of this drug?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Inhaled therapy for hospital-acquired pneumonia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intramuscular therapy for infective endocarditis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intravenous therapy for MRSA bloodstream infection

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral therapy for severe antibiotic-associated colitis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Topical ointment for superficial skin infections

explanation.summary: Bacitracin is typically used as an ointment for superficial skin infections.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bacitracin is a peptidoglycan-inhibitor antibiotic that is typically used as an ointment for superficial skin infections. Vancomycin, the other drug in this brick, is the one given intravenously for serious staphylococcal infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bacitracin is not described as an inhaled agent for pneumonia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Deep-seated infections such as endocarditis are not treated with a topical agent like bacitracin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Intravenous therapy for serious MRSA infection is the role of vancomycin, not bacitracin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oral therapy for colitis is not the use of bacitracin described in this brick.

questions.stem: A pharmacology student examines the core scaffold shared by penicillin G, amoxicillin, and nafcillin. Every one of these agents is built on a strained four-membered ring fused to a five-membered sulfur-containing ring, and an amide and a carboxylic acid group are also present. Which of the following pairs of rings makes up this shared core?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A beta-lactam ring fused to a dihydrothiazine ring

choices.label: B
choices.text: A beta-lactam ring fused to a thiazolidine ring

choices.label: C
choices.text: A beta-lactam ring fused to an imidazolidine ring

choices.label: D
choices.text: A macrolactone ring fused to a pyrrolidine ring

choices.label: E
choices.text: A macrolactone ring fused to a thiazolidine ring

explanation.summary: The penicillin nucleus is a beta-lactam ring fused to a thiazolidine ring.
explanation.whyCorrect: Penicillin structure consists of a fused beta-lactam ring, which is why these drugs are called beta-lactam antibiotics, joined to a thiazolidine ring that carries two methyl groups and a carboxylic acid. An amide side chain projects from the beta-lactam ring. This chemistry matters clinically because it determines both antibacterial activity and the hypersensitivity reactions penicillins can provoke.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A dihydrothiazine ring is not the ring fused to the beta-lactam nucleus of a penicillin; the penicillin partner ring is the five-membered thiazolidine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An imidazolidine ring is nitrogen-based and is not the sulfur-containing ring fused to the penicillin beta-lactam.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neither a macrolactone nor a pyrrolidine ring forms part of the penicillin nucleus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The penicillin core is not a macrolactone; a large lactone ring belongs to a different antibiotic class entirely and is not described for penicillins.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with streptococcal pharyngitis is treated with an oral beta-lactam. The drug halts construction of the bacterial cell wall by irreversibly blocking the enzyme that cross-links the linear peptidoglycan chains. Inhibition of which of the following enzymes accounts for this effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dihydrofolate reductase of the folate pathway

choices.label: B
choices.text: DNA gyrase, a bacterial topoisomerase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Peptidyl transferase of the 50S ribosomal subunit

choices.label: D
choices.text: RNA polymerase of the bacterial cytoplasm

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transpeptidase, a penicillin-binding protein

explanation.summary: Penicillins irreversibly inhibit transpeptidase (penicillin-binding protein), the cross-linking enzyme of peptidoglycan.
explanation.whyCorrect: The beta-lactam ring binds to and irreversibly, noncompetitively inhibits transpeptidase, also called penicillin-binding protein (PBP). This enzyme cross-links the linear peptidoglycan chains of the cell wall. With cross-linking blocked, cell wall synthesis is halted and the bacteria die.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dihydrofolate reductase blockade interferes with folate synthesis, not with peptidoglycan cross-linking.
whyWrongByChoice.B: DNA gyrase inhibition is the mechanism of a different antibiotic class and has nothing to do with the beta-lactam ring.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Peptidyl transferase is a ribosomal activity; protein synthesis inhibition is a mechanism of other antibiotic classes, not of beta-lactams.
whyWrongByChoice.D: RNA polymerase inhibition blocks transcription; penicillins do not act on bacterial RNA synthesis.

questions.stem: The beta-lactam ring of penicillin occupies the active site of the enzyme that cross-links peptidoglycan because it imitates a component of the growing cell wall. The beta-lactam ring acts as a structural analogue of which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: D-Ala-D-Ala

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lipoteichoic acid

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mycolic acid

choices.label: D
choices.text: N-acetylglucosamine

choices.label: E
choices.text: N-acetylmuramic acid

explanation.summary: The beta-lactam ring mimics D-Ala-D-Ala, the peptidoglycan residue that transpeptidase normally engages.
explanation.whyCorrect: The beta-lactam ring is a structural analogue of D-Ala-D-Ala, which is found in the peptidoglycan and normally binds to transpeptidase (PBP). By occupying that binding site, the antibiotic blocks peptidoglycan cross-linking in the cell wall.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lipoteichoic acid is a gram-positive wall component that is not involved in the transpeptidase reaction targeted by penicillins.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mycolic acid is a mycobacterial wall lipid and has no role in the peptidoglycan cross-linking step blocked here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: N-acetylglucosamine alternates with N-acetylmuramic acid in the glycan backbone but is not the transpeptidase substrate mimicked by the drug.
whyWrongByChoice.E: N-acetylmuramic acid is a sugar backbone unit of peptidoglycan, not the residue that the beta-lactam ring imitates.

questions.stem: Exposure to a beta-lactam antibiotic causes a gram-positive organism not only to stop building new cell wall but also to rapidly digest the wall it already has, producing lesions and osmotic death. Activation of which of the following best explains this additional killing effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autolysins present within the bacterial cell wall

choices.label: B
choices.text: Beta-lactamases held within the periplasmic space

choices.label: C
choices.text: Efflux pumps situated in the plasma membrane

choices.label: D
choices.text: Porin channels within the outer cell membrane

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transpeptidases acting at the cross-linking site

explanation.summary: Beta-lactams activate autolysins, which digest the cell wall and cause osmotic death.
explanation.whyCorrect: Autolysins exist in the cell wall, predominantly in gram-positive bacteria, where they normally remodel the wall during growth under tight regulation. Beta-lactams, acting in synergy with accumulated cell wall building blocks, release that regulation and activate the autolysins, which rapidly digest the wall. The result is osmotic death, part of the bactericidal effect of these drugs.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Beta-lactamases destroy the antibiotic and protect the organism; they do not digest the bacterium's own cell wall.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Efflux pumps expel drug from the cell and play no part in digesting the peptidoglycan wall.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Porins are entry channels in gram-negative outer membranes; altering them affects drug access, not wall digestion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transpeptidases build cross-links and are inhibited by the drug, so their activity is decreased rather than activated.

questions.stem: A researcher shows that penicillin G efficiently kills a broth culture of Streptococcus pyogenes during log-phase growth but has almost no killing effect on the same organism held in stationary phase. Which of the following best explains this observation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Beta-lactamase output rises sharply in stationary phase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cell wall synthesis occurs only in actively multiplying bacteria

choices.label: C
choices.text: Penicillins are bacteriostatic rather than bactericidal drugs

choices.label: D
choices.text: Porin channels close whenever bacterial growth slows

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ribosomal drug targets are exposed only in dividing cells

explanation.summary: Penicillins kill only during rapid growth, because only then is cell wall actively being built.
explanation.whyCorrect: Penicillin action depends on the rapid growth of bacteria both in vitro and in vivo. For bacteria to grow, cell walls must be built; if cell wall synthesis is inhibited, growth is halted. These drugs are bactericidal, but they can only kill during rapid growth, when the organisms are actively multiplying.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Nothing in the pharmacology of penicillins ties beta-lactamase output to growth phase; the explanation is the absence of wall synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Penicillins are bactericidal, not bacteriostatic; the limitation is when they can kill, not whether they kill.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Porin changes are a resistance mechanism in some gram-negative rods, not a growth-phase phenomenon in a gram-positive coccus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Penicillins do not act on the ribosome at all, so ribosomal target exposure is irrelevant.

questions.stem: Penicillins are bactericidal at concentrations that are essentially nontoxic to human cells. Which of the following best explains this selective toxicity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Human cells divide too slowly to be injured by the drug

choices.label: B
choices.text: Human cells exclude penicillin by means of efflux pumps

choices.label: C
choices.text: Human cells neither make nor require peptidoglycan

choices.label: D
choices.text: Human cells produce an intracellular beta-lactamase enzyme

choices.label: E
choices.text: Human cells rapidly metabolize penicillin to an inert form

explanation.summary: Penicillins spare host cells because human cells have no peptidoglycan to target.
explanation.whyCorrect: The target of penicillins is the cross-linking of peptidoglycan in the bacterial cell wall. Penicillins do not damage host cells because human cells neither make nor need peptidoglycan, so the drug has no equivalent target in the patient.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Growth rate of human cells is not the relevant factor; the absence of the drug target is.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Host efflux of the drug is not the described basis for selective toxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Beta-lactamase is a bacterial resistance enzyme, not a protective human enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Penicillins are polar compounds that are not metabolized extensively; host metabolism is not the basis of their safety.

questions.stem: Penicillin G, the antistaphylococcal penicillins, and the aminopenicillins differ from one another in spectrum, acid stability, and susceptibility to beta-lactamases, yet all are built on an identical bicyclic nucleus. These differences are produced mainly by modifying which portion of the molecule?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The carbonyl carbon within the beta-lactam ring

choices.label: B
choices.text: The nitrogen atom within the beta-lactam ring

choices.label: C
choices.text: The side chain (R) group attached to the amide

choices.label: D
choices.text: The sulfur atom within the thiazolidine ring

choices.label: E
choices.text: The two methyl groups on the thiazolidine ring

explanation.summary: Penicillins differ chiefly in the R side chain of the amide group.
explanation.whyCorrect: Variation among the penicillins is mainly limited to the side chain (R) group of the amide. Altering this side chain is what changes acid stability, spectrum, and resistance to beta-lactamases across the subgroups. Separately, prodrugs have been developed by modifying the carboxylic acid group.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The beta-lactam carbonyl is essential for binding transpeptidase and is not what is varied between agents.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The beta-lactam nitrogen is part of the ring that must stay intact for activity, not a site of structural variation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The sulfur of the thiazolidine ring is part of the conserved nucleus shared by all penicillins.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The two methyl groups on the thiazolidine ring are conserved features of the penicillin nucleus.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old woman with mild streptococcal pharyngitis is to be treated with an oral penicillin. Penicillin G is avoided in favor of penicillin V. Which property of penicillin V best accounts for this choice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It covers the gram-negative rods that penicillin G misses

choices.label: B
choices.text: It has a far longer plasma half-life than penicillin G

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is more stable in gastric acid than penicillin G

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is not hydrolyzed by staphylococcal beta-lactamases

choices.label: E
choices.text: It reaches higher CSF concentrations than penicillin G

explanation.summary: Penicillin V is acid stable and therefore orally absorbed, whereas penicillin G is destroyed by gastric acid.
explanation.whyCorrect: Penicillins vary in their resistance to gastric acid and therefore in oral bioavailability. Penicillin G is poorly absorbed orally because it is broken down by gastric acid in the stomach, while penicillin V has increased absorption owing to its increased acid stability. That makes penicillin V the practical oral choice.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Penicillin V shares the narrow gram-positive spectrum of penicillin G and has little activity against gram-negative rods.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Plasma half-lives of most penicillins are similar, in the range of 30 minutes to 1 hour.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Resistance to staphylococcal beta-lactamases belongs to the antistaphylococcal penicillins such as nafcillin and oxacillin, not to penicillin V.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Penicillins cross into the CNS chiefly when the meninges are inflamed; penicillin V is not distinguished by CSF penetration.

questions.stem: Most penicillins are eliminated unchanged by the kidney. One beta-lactamase-resistant penicillin is instead eliminated mainly in the bile, a point that matters when choosing an agent for a patient with poor renal function. Which of the following is that agent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amoxicillin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ampicillin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nafcillin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Penicillin G

choices.label: E
choices.text: Piperacillin

explanation.summary: Nafcillin, a beta-lactamase-resistant penicillin, is excreted mainly in the bile.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nafcillin is an antistaphylococcal penicillin that resists staphylococcal beta-lactamases. Unlike the other penicillins, which are usually excreted unchanged in the urine by glomerular filtration and tubular secretion, nafcillin is mainly excreted in the bile. It also has poor oral absorption.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amoxicillin is an aminopenicillin, is not beta-lactamase resistant, and is renally eliminated.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ampicillin is renally excreted; it is distinguished instead by undergoing enterohepatic recycling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Penicillin G is excreted unchanged in the urine and is readily hydrolyzed by beta-lactamases.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Piperacillin is an antipseudomonal penicillin given parenterally and is not the biliary-excreted agent described.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man with bacterial meningitis achieves therapeutic CSF concentrations on an intravenous penicillin. Once his meningeal inflammation resolves, the same dose would yield markedly lower CSF levels. Which of the following best explains the difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Inflammation activates a pump that drives penicillin into the CSF

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inflammation allows penicillin to cross the blood-brain barrier

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inflammation increases hepatic conversion of penicillin prodrug

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inflammation sharply raises CSF protein binding of penicillin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inflammation slows the renal tubular secretion of penicillin

explanation.summary: Penicillins penetrate the CNS only when the meninges are inflamed.
explanation.whyCorrect: Penicillins are widely distributed in the body, and most cross the blood-brain barrier to penetrate the central nervous system, but only when the meninges are inflamed. Once inflammation resolves, the barrier again restricts entry and CSF concentrations fall at any given dose.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Active transport of penicillin at the CNS interface moves drug out of the CSF into the bloodstream, not into the CSF.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Penicillins are polar compounds that are not metabolized extensively, so hepatic activation is not involved.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased CSF protein binding is not the described mechanism of CNS penetration for penicillins.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Renal tubular secretion governs systemic elimination, not the ability of drug to enter the CSF.

questions.stem: A patient with markedly reduced creatinine clearance is started on high-dose intravenous penicillin G and rapidly accumulates the drug. Which route of elimination normally handles this drug and accounts for the accumulation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conjugation with glucuronide and biliary export

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glomerular filtration and renal tubular secretion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hepatic oxidation by cytochrome P450 enzymes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hydrolysis by circulating plasma esterase enzymes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sequestration and slow release from adipose tissue

explanation.summary: Penicillins are excreted unchanged in the urine by glomerular filtration and tubular secretion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Penicillins are usually excreted unchanged in the urine via glomerular filtration and tubular secretion. They are polar compounds and are not metabolized extensively, so a fall in renal clearance directly raises drug concentrations.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Biliary excretion is the exception rather than the rule and applies chiefly to nafcillin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Penicillins are not extensively metabolized, so hepatic oxidation is not the principal route of elimination.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Plasma esterase hydrolysis is not described as an elimination route for penicillins.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Penicillins are polar compounds and are not stored in fat.

questions.stem: Among the penicillins, one agent is notable for being returned to the circulation after biliary excretion and reabsorption from the gut, a cycle that prolongs its intestinal exposure. Which of the following agents undergoes this enterohepatic recycling?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ampicillin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nafcillin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oxacillin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Penicillin G

choices.label: E
choices.text: Penicillin V

explanation.summary: Ampicillin is the penicillin that undergoes enterohepatic recycling.
explanation.whyCorrect: Penicillin itself does not undergo enterohepatic recycling; it is ampicillin that does. Ampicillin is an aminopenicillin with increased stability to gastric acid, and it is also the penicillin most associated with nausea and diarrhea, consistent with prolonged exposure of the gut to drug.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Nafcillin is excreted mainly in the bile but is not the agent described as undergoing enterohepatic recycling.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oxacillin is an antistaphylococcal penicillin and is not associated with this cycle.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Penicillin G is poorly absorbed orally and is excreted unchanged in the urine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Penicillin V is distinguished by acid stability and good oral absorption, not by enterohepatic recycling.
